specPoints.text: describe these experimental techniques for the separation of mixtures: simple distillation, fractional distillation, filtration, crystallisation, paper chromatography

primer.text: You already know from Element, Compound or Mixture that mixtures come apart by physical means. This note tours the five techniques the syllabus names — simple distillation, fractional distillation, filtration, crystallisation and paper chromatography — and matches each one to the kind of mixture it separates best.

lessons.title: Distillation: Simple and Fractional
lessons.opening: Distillation separates the part of a solution that boils off: heat the flask, the vapour rises into the condenser, and the liquid drips out pure while the dissolved solid stays behind. Simple distillation handles one liquid from a solution, or a pure liquid from a blend; fractional distillation handles two or more miscible liquids by boiling out the more volatile one first.
keyPoints: Simple distillation separates the liquid from a solution, leaving the dissolved solid behind in the flask.
In the condenser, vapour cools and condenses into the pure liquid, which collects in a beaker.
Condenser water enters at the bottom, near the collecting beaker, and leaves at the top.
Fractional distillation separates a pair of miscible liquids, or several, by their boiling points.
Heat the mixture to the lowest boiling point present; that substance boils first and distils out.
With ethanol and water, collect the ethanol at 78 °C and stop heating when the thermometer reaches 100 °C.

low.restatement: Simple distillation: heat a solution, catch the vapour in a condenser, and the pure liquid drips into the beaker while the solid stays. Fractional distillation: same idea, but for two miscible liquids — boil off the one with the lower boiling point first.
low.analogy: Simple distillation is like catching steam from a kettle on a cold lid: the water escapes as vapour and returns as clean drops, leaving anything dissolved in the kettle.
low.examPointer: Diagram marks live in the details: water in at the condenser bottom near the beaker, out at the top near the column.

medium.restatement: Simple distillation recovers the liquid from a solution — the solvent evaporates, travels through the condenser, condenses and is collected, and only the solid solute remains in the flask. Fractional distillation applies the same condenser trick to two or more miscible liquids: hold the temperature at the lowest boiling point present, collect that substance completely, and stop heating when the thermometer climbs towards the next one.
medium.analogy: Think of a relay where the lightest runner goes first: heat to the fastest-boiling substance's temperature, let it finish its leg, then pull the baton before the next one starts.
medium.examPointer: Ethanol boils at 78 °C and water at 100 °C; collect ethanol first and stop at 100 °C.

check.stem: Salt water is heated in simple distillation. What is collected in the beaker, and what is left in the flask?

options.text: Pure water collects in the beaker; the salt stays in the flask
options.explanation: Only the liquid boils off and condenses; the dissolved solid cannot evaporate.

options.text: Salt collects in the beaker; water stays in the flask
options.explanation: The vapour that rises is water, so water is what the condenser delivers to the beaker.

options.text: Both collect in the beaker as salt water
options.explanation: Distillation separates; the beaker receives the condensed liquid only.

options.text: Nothing collects until the salt boils too
options.explanation: Heating stops once the liquid has gone; the salt never boils.

check.stem: In a labelled diagram of simple distillation, where must the cooling water enter?

options.text: At the bottom of the condenser, near the collecting beaker
options.explanation: Water entering low fills the cooling jacket against the vapour flow and chills the whole condenser.

options.text: At the top of the condenser, near the column
options.explanation: That is where water leaves; entering high leaves the lower jacket uncooled.

options.text: Into the flask, to speed the boiling
options.explanation: Cooling water belongs to the condenser jacket, not the boiling flask.

options.text: Anywhere, since the direction makes no difference
options.explanation: Diagrams are marked on the correct direction, as the exam hint stresses.

check.stem: Ethanol and water mix completely. Which technique separates them, and how is it run?

options.text: Fractional distillation: hold 78 °C to boil off the ethanol, then stop before 100 °C
options.explanation: The lower boiling point leaves first; stopping at 100 °C keeps water out of the beaker.

options.text: Filtration: ethanol passes through, water is caught
options.explanation: Both are liquids; there is no undissolved solid for filter paper to catch.

options.text: Simple distillation: collect both liquids in one beaker
options.explanation: One beaker of mixed distillate is no separation at all.

options.text: Crystallisation: cool until ethanol crystals form
options.explanation: Ethanol does not crystallise from the mixture; it boils at 78 °C.

check.stem: During fractional distillation of ethanol and water, the thermometer climbs from 78 °C towards 100 °C. What should the operator do?

options.text: Stop heating — the ethanol has all been collected
options.explanation: A rising temperature means the low-boiling substance is gone and water is next.

options.text: Increase the heat to finish faster
options.explanation: More heat brings water over and ruins the separation.

options.text: Swap the beaker and keep collecting the same liquid
options.explanation: The distillate is already the ethanol; continuing collects water into it.

options.text: Add cold water to the mixture
options.explanation: Dilution does not separate anything.

check.stem: What does miscible mean, and why does it rule out filtration for an ethanol-water mixture?

options.text: The liquids mix with no boundary, so no solid exists for filter paper to catch
options.explanation: Filtration needs an undissolved solid; two liquids that blend have none.

options.text: The liquids have equal densities, so they cannot be separated at all
options.explanation: Density equality is irrelevant; boiling points do the separating.

options.text: The liquids react into a compound, so distillation is barred
options.explanation: Miscible liquids still blend physically; nothing new is formed.

options.text: The liquids must first be frozen to separate them
options.explanation: The separation runs on boiling point differences, not freezing.

lessons.title: Filtration, Crystallisation and Chromatography
lessons.opening: Filtration, crystallisation and paper chromatography complete the physical toolkit. Filtration catches an undissolved solid on filter paper; crystallisation grows pure crystals out of a cooling, saturating solution; and chromatography lets dissolved substances race up paper at different speeds so the components show up as separate spots.
keyPoints: Filtration separates an undissolved solid from its liquid using filter paper in a funnel.
The liquid that passes through is the filtrate; the solid left on the paper is the residue.
Crystallisation recovers a dissolved solid whose solubility falls as the hot solution cools.
Dip a cold, clean glass rod in; crystals forming on it show the solution is saturated.
Paper chromatography separates dissolved substances by the different distances they travel with a solvent.
More soluble substances travel further up the paper; the pencil line stays above the solvent level.

low.restatement: Filtration sieves an undissolved solid out of its liquid: filtrate through, residue on the paper. Crystallisation evaporates some solvent, tests with a cold rod whether the solution is saturated, then cools it so crystals grow, and the crystals are washed and dried.
low.analogy: Crystallisation is like making rock candy on a string: as the sugary water cools, the sugar can no longer stay dissolved and builds solid crystals.
low.examPointer: Paper chromatography: pencil line above the solvent, higher solubility travels further.

medium.restatement: Filtration works because only particles small enough to slip through the paper join the filtrate, while the large solid particles stay behind as residue. Crystallisation suits a solid far more soluble in hot solvent than in cold: evaporate the solvent until a cold rod test shows the solution is saturated, cool slowly so crystals grow as solubility falls, then filter, wash with cold distilled water and dry.
medium.analogy: A sieve sorts pasta from water on size alone; chromatography is a race where each runner's grip on the track — their solubility — sets how far they get.
medium.examPointer: Name the parts: filtrate passes, residue stays; crystals come from cooling a saturated solution.

check.stem: Sand is stirred into water. Which technique recovers the sand, and what is the sand left on the paper called?

options.text: Filtration; the sand left on the paper is the residue
options.explanation: Undissolved solids stay on the paper as residue while the filtrate passes.

options.text: Filtration; the sand in the beaker below is the filtrate
options.explanation: The filtrate is the liquid that passed through, not the solid caught.

options.text: Simple distillation; the sand boils off first
options.explanation: Sand is a solid with no boiling point to exploit here.

options.text: Crystallisation; the sand grows crystals
options.explanation: Crystals grow from dissolved solids; sand never dissolved.

check.stem: How does a cold glass rod test whether a solution is ready for crystallisation?

options.text: Dip a clean, dry, cold rod in; crystals forming on it show the solution is saturated
options.explanation: A saturated solution deposits crystals on a cold surface straight away.

options.text: The rod dissolves if the solution is saturated
options.explanation: Glass does not dissolve; the rod is an observation tool.

options.text: The rod changes colour when crystals are near
options.explanation: The signal is crystal growth on the rod, not a colour change.

options.text: Stir with the rod; faster stirring proves saturation
options.explanation: Stirring changes nothing about how much is dissolved.

check.stem: Why does crystallisation need a solid that is much more soluble in hot solvent than in cold?

options.text: The gap lets crystals grow as the solution cools and keeps them from redissolving
options.explanation: Falling solubility on cooling drives the solid out of solution as crystals.

options.text: Hot solvent sterilises the crystals
options.explanation: The technique rests on solubility differences, not hygiene.

options.text: Cold solvent would boil instead
options.explanation: Cooling is applied after heating; nothing boils during crystallisation.

options.text: The solid must melt before it can crystallise
options.explanation: Crystals form from solution; melting the solid is not part of the method.

check.stem: In paper chromatography, why must the pencil line sit above the solvent level at the start?

options.text: So the samples do not wash off the line into the solvent container
options.explanation: Submerged spots dissolve away into the solvent instead of travelling up the paper.

options.text: So the solvent cannot evaporate
options.explanation: Line placement has no effect on evaporation.

options.text: So the pencil does not run into the chromatogram
options.explanation: Pencil is chosen precisely because it does not run; the depth rule protects the samples.

options.text: Because spots below the line travel faster
options.explanation: Travel distance depends on solubility, not on starting depth.

check.stem: Why is the starting line drawn in pencil rather than ink?

options.text: Pencil does not dissolve, so it will not run up the paper with the samples
options.explanation: Ink would travel with the solvent and confuse the results.

options.text: Pencil marks are darker and easier to see
options.explanation: Visibility is not the reason; chemical inertness in the solvent is.

options.text: Ink would make the paper too heavy
options.explanation: Paper mass is irrelevant.

options.text: Pencil is the only colour allowed under exam rules
options.explanation: The rule is chemical: inks dissolve and would join the separation.

glossary.definition: Separating a liquid from a solution by boiling it off and condensing the vapour.
The glass tube that cools vapour back into liquid during distillation.
Describes liquids that mix into each other completely, with no boundary between them.
Separating an undissolved solid from a liquid by pouring the mixture through filter paper.
The liquid that passes through the filter paper.
The solid left behind on the filter paper.
Recovering a dissolved solid by evaporating solvent and cooling the solution so crystals grow.
A solution holding all the dissolved solid it can at that temperature.

workedExample.prompt: Sodium chloride is a soluble solid. Which technique separates a soluble solid from a solution: filtration, simple distillation, crystallisation, or chromatography?
steps: The question asks for the solid from the solution, not the liquid.
A soluble solid is recovered by gently heating the solution until the solvent evaporates and the solid crystallises out.
Simple distillation would instead collect the liquid, and filtration only works on an undissolved solid.
